newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin follows doctors' orders, limits workload.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin follows doctors' orders, limits workload.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, following strict doctors' orders as he prepares for heart surgery, is spending two or three hours a day on paperwork, press spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said on Friday.
"He has a work schedule of two or three hours a day," Yastrzhembsky told a news conference.

Doctors said on Wednesday that Yeltsin, 65, was fit enough for a heart operation, but that surgery would be postponed for at least six weeks. The operation -- a relatively routine bypass operation -- will improve the blood supply to Yeltsin's heart.
The president has been in the Central Clinical Hospital since September 13 and doctors expect him to stay there until the operation.

Yastrzhembsky said little had changed since doctors spoke to journalists on Wednesday. "For now he is in the Central Clinical Hospital. You have heard everything, there has been no lack of information, nothing essentially new has happened since then.
Yeltsin had two heart attacks last year and doctors say he may have had another one between the two rounds of Russia's presidential election in which he was re-elected for a new four-year term.
He announced his decision to undergo heart surgery in a television interview on September 5, breaking a long Kremlin tradition of secrecy about the health of Russian leaders.
An opinion poll published by Interfax news agency on Friday said a majority of those questioned approved of Yeltsin's decision to come clean about his health and admit to the need for heart surgery.
The survey by the respected Public Opinion agency said 60 percent of respondents praised Yeltsin's openness while 17 percent were not in favour of it. Others had no definite opinion or did not care.

Another opinion poll by the VTsIOM organisation said that more than two thirds of people it surveyed believed that Yeltsin had completely or partially relinquished control over the government and his own administration.

But less than a third of respondents believed this could lead to unrest or instability and more than a half thought important decisions could be made without Yeltsin, according to the VTsIOM data published in the Sevodnya newspaper.
Russian security chief Alexander Lebed and Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov painted a picture of looming instability and chaos on Thursday.

Lebed, known for blunt, outspoken remarks, told a news conference that the decision-making process in the world's largest country had virtually ground to a halt and some regions were teetering on the brink of disaster.
"We are at a dangerous limit, a very dangerous limit. It is not a time to fight. We must get out of the abyss," he said.
He warned of discontent in the army over unpaid wages. "If some serious measures are not taken, we will have a very hot October," he said.
Zyuganov, on a visit to France, called on Yeltsin to resign.
"If one thinks of the interests of Mr Yeltsin himself, of his family and of Russia, it would be much better for him to resign," Zyuganov told the French Institute for International Relations.
Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin's constitutional stand-in, has dismissed talk of Yeltsin resigning. Doctors say the president should make a complete recovery after his bypass surgery.
